title: NHS England Approves First Drug to Help Multiple Sclerosis Patients Walk
excerpt: Fampridine, a twice-daily pill that improves walking speed in up to 43 percent of patients, becomes available on the NHS in England from Thursday — years after Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
body:
• Fampridine, the first medicine designed to improve walking in adults with multiple sclerosis, is now available on the NHS in England from July 23, 2026.
  • Clinical trials showed the twice-daily pill improved walking speed in 43 percent of patients by helping damaged nerves transmit electrical signals more effectively.
  • About 5,000 of the 120,000 people living with MS in England will be eligible in the first year.
  • England is the last UK nation to approve fampridine — Wales began offering it in 2019, Scotland in 2020, and Northern Ireland in 2023.

Thousands of people living with multiple sclerosis in England will gain access to a drug described as “life-changing” after NHS England approved fampridine, the first medicine specifically designed to improve walking in adults with the condition.

The twice-daily pill, available from Thursday under the brand name Fampyra, works by boosting electrical signals along nerves damaged by MS, helping them travel to muscles more effectively. About 5,000 patients will be eligible in the first year, with the drug expected to help them walk more easily and maintain independence for longer.

How Fampridine Works

Multiple sclerosis damages the myelin sheath that protects nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord, disrupting the electrical signals that control movement. Fampridine is a potassium channel blocker that targets this damage, allowing nerve impulses to pass through demyelinated areas more efficiently.

In clinical trials, the drug improved walking speed in 43 percent of patients, according to data cited by NHS England. Eligible patients will initially take fampridine for two to four weeks. If their walking improves, they continue the treatment for as long as it remains effective, with regular reviews.

“For people with MS who have spent years relying on physiotherapy, walking aids or help from others, having access to a one-of-a-kind treatment specifically for walking difficulties offers real hope of greater independence.”

— Professor James Palmer, National Medical Director for Specialised Services, NHS England

England Was the Last to Approve

The approval brings England in line with the rest of the United Kingdom, ending years of unequal access. Wales first approved fampridine in 2019, followed by Scotland in 2020 and Northern Ireland in 2023. NHS England’s delay followed a 2022 decision by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) not to recommend the drug, which it deemed not cost-effective.

The MS Society and MS Trust campaigned for years to reverse that decision. After NHS England committed to reconsidering fampridine through its own process in late 2024, delays over funding pushed the final approval to July 2026.

“We welcome NHS England’s decision to recommend fampridine for people living with MS in England,” said Lucy Taylor, CEO of the MS Trust. “This recommendation is a significant step towards ensuring people with MS have equitable access to effective treatments across the whole of the UK.”

Patient Impact

Aysen Slack, 65, from Eastbourne, previously paid for fampridine privately before stopping due to the cost. “Fampridine seemed to be working well for me but paying for the medication was a significant expense, and I could not keep doing that forever,” she told The Times. “My mobility has decreased a lot and even in my flat I have to use sticks now. It would make a huge difference to my life if I were able to improve my walking.”

More than 120,000 people live with MS in England. To be eligible for fampridine, patients must have walking problems caused by MS with an Expanded Disability Status Scale score between 4 and 7 — meaning those who can walk up to 500 metres without aid on one end, and those who require a wheelchair for most mobility on the other.

What Comes Next

Professor Frankie Swords, NHS England’s national medical director, said the drug could be “life-changing” for thousands of patients. “Fampridine helps electrical messages travel along nerves damaged by MS, giving people the chance to walk more easily and helping them be more mobile to do more of the everyday things that matter to them,” she said.

The MS Society noted that setting up monitoring and assessment services across England will take time, as it did in other UK nations. Ceri Smith, the charity’s head of policy, called on NHS services to ensure fampridine reaches “all people with MS who could benefit from it, regardless of where in England they live.”
